samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers are accurate, own the mistake plainly, give the refund dates, and handle the overdraft fee without promising reimbursement. B's first sentence states the 2 March date and the $29 amount more directly, but B also adds 'The only problem was the second charge,' a claim the fact sheet doesn't support. A sticks strictly to the sheet, and its banner also tells owners to email about bank fees. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers stick closely to the fact sheet. Each one owns the duplicate billing run, gives the 4 March and 11 March refund dates, says owners don't need to do anything, and treats overdraft fees only as something to reply about. A's opening sentence states the date and the $29 sooner, and its note about taking the banner down after 11 March is useful, but it adds a claim the sheet doesn't support: 'The only problem was the second charge.' B avoids that addition and its banner also points owners with bank fees to the support email, so the two even out.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): The two emails are almost the same: both are accurate, own the mistake plainly, give the refund dates, ask nothing of the owner, and handle overdraft fees correctly. B's banner is better. It says 'We charged you $29 twice' to the account owner, while A's banner shifts to the passive 'A billing error… charged some accounts', which reads oddly on an affected owner's own billing page. B also adds the useful note that the banner should only show on affected accounts. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both emails follow the fact sheet closely: each opens with the double $29 charge, names the billing job running twice as Shiftwell's fault, gives the 4 March and 11 March refund dates, says owners need do nothing, and handles overdraft fees as reply-and-review without promising reimbursement. A's banner is tighter and stays in the active voice ('We charged you $29 twice'), while B's banner says 'A billing error... charged some accounts' and so does not plainly say Shiftwell caused it. B also repeats the apology. B's note about not claiming the bug is fixed is thoughtful, but A is slightly cleaner overall.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B's email opens with the money: 'On 2 March, we charged your Shiftwell subscription twice.' A starts with 'We made a mistake' before saying what happened to the charge. Both answers state the cause and the refund dates correctly and handle the overdraft fee without promising it. A's banner shifts to the passive 'a billing error' and adds 'automatically', which the fact sheet doesn't say, while B stays a little tighter to the facts. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Answer A opens with the money fact: the reader was charged twice on 2 March. It names Shiftwell's billing job as the cause in active voice, and its banner stands on its own, covering the refund date, no action needed and the bank-fee route. Answer B is accurate and well organised, but it opens with company talk ('We made a mistake') before the money fact. Its banner also softens to 'You may have been charged' and the passive 'A billing error', and the email adds a sentimental line that isn't on the fact sheet.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A is shorter and plainer. It names the loss and the fault directly, gives one clear upload action, and puts placeholders on the delivery estimate and the remedy. B is also careful and honest, but it leans on stock empathy phrases like "we know how much this book means" and "added hurt... at an already painful time" and spreads the next steps over several paragraphs. A's acknowledgment of what the book was for is a little oblique, but overall A better fits a message for someone who is grieving. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers name the loss plainly, say Loomprint caused it, and use placeholders for remedies that haven't been decided rather than inventing them. B also writes the order-page notice the request asked for, adds the useful "your book hasn't been printed / nothing you did caused it," and stays tighter. pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A is short, plain and personal. It names the loss and admits fault, gives one clear re-upload action and marks undecided facts with brackets; its only stretch is saying the reprint costs nothing extra. B is caring and its notes are useful, but it is longer and leans on stock phrases ('a moment that matters deeply', 'at a time like this', 'deepest apologies and sympathy'). It also offers several routes instead of one clear action and uses bold headers that feel like a template. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers say plainly that Loomprint lost the print files and that it was Loomprint's mistake, and neither uses exclamation marks or marketing lines. B is shorter and more personal. It covers the book's purpose in one plain sentence, gives a single clear re-upload button and adds a matching order-page banner. B slightly overreaches with 'we'll cover the reprint… you won't pay anything extra', which the brief doesn't strictly state, while A puts any extra offer behind a clearly marked placeholder.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers refuse to say 'fully resolved', avoid opening with boilerplate reassurance, and give clear password steps with a link. B's email says, without that condition, that there is 'no indication so far' that notes were accessed, which is unverified reassurance, and B skips the in-app version. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Neither answer says the issue is resolved, and neither uses an unverified 'no evidence of misuse' line; B allows that line only if it has been checked, and says so in its brackets. B gives both the in-app banner and the email, as the request asked, and marks unverified claims, such as notes not being in the database, as items to confirm. A's separate 'What we don't know yet' section is a strength, but both answers spend several sentences explaining why the CEO's phrases were left out, where the rubric asks for one line.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers handle the record, bookmark, more-options and heart fixes well. Both keep the 'Favourite' name constant, expose the toggle state programmatically, and say not to also change the label. B wins narrowly on item 2: it gives the short 'Trim' (and 'Stop' as an option) and states outright that names must not include 'button' or 'icon'. A uses longer names and never states that rule. B loses some concision with its general-notes section and makes one odd claim, that 'the role is also missing from the name'. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give the right names for the record, bookmark and overflow controls. Both fix the heart with one constant name plus a programmatic toggle state. B says outright not to combine a changing label with a toggle state. A wrongly says the role is 'missing from the name' for the stop control, which contradicts its own advice, offers two names for that control, and adds a general-notes section that drifts into a broader lecture. A does state the rule against putting 'button' or 'icon' in a name more clearly, but B is cleaner overall, though 'Stop recording' and 'Trim recording' are longer than needed.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): The two answers are nearly identical in substance. pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers fix every control well and choose the toggle-state approach for the heart without also changing its name. A's 'Trim' is closer to the short action names the rubric asks for, but A offers two names for some controls and adds unrelated advice on touch targets, focus order and WCAG. pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B says plainly that the card was declined and the plan was not renewed. It names the action on its button and makes up nothing, using a placeholder for the access policy. It also guesses at causes of the decline (an expired card, the bank) and puts an unconfirmed grace period in the copy itself, which is worse than B's missing cheek. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A says plainly that the card was declined and the plan hasn't renewed, uses a clear 'Update card' button, and leaves a placeholder for the access policy instead of making one up.
